newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's agent says premium rates still falling.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's agent says premium rates still falling.

text.p: Premium rates in almost all classes of insurance business are continuing to deteriorate, Lloyd's of London member's agent Christie Brockbank Shipton Ltd (CBSL) said on Thursday.
The latest CBSL Market Rate indices for May show a weakening pattern across the market and contrary to reports of rising premiums in motor, CBSL sees little evidence of rate increases.
A lack of significant major claims is partly responsible for the softening of the insurance markets as a whole but is leading to favourable forecasts on open years.
The final 1994 figures ended up very close to forecasts and 1995 is expected to continue to improve.
The lack of resistance to rate cutting in all areas of marine is unlikely to improve in the short term, says CBSL, while non-marine is also very competitive.
The global airline premium for 1997 is anticipated to fall again during the year as competition for market share increases and this is likely to affect the liability and general aviation markets.
According to CBSL members' agents significantly outperformed Lloyd's Investment Trusts (LITs) in the 1994 year.
LITs average 9.23 percent compared to the average agents' Members' Agent Pooling Arrangement (MAPA) underwriting result of 11.07 percent.
"The supposed highly sophisticated new investors do not appear to have beaten the traditional members' agents at their own game," says CBSL.

"Members agents' cynicism arising from close involvement in the past may enable them to recognise a "deja vu" situation more ruthlessly than the new corporate investor. One may question whether the Trusts are buying the best advice available," it suggests.

On the question of the possible abolition of the annual venture - where the market's traditional backers, Names, form syndicates anew every year - CBSL suggest its demise may be a foregone conclusion.
"The impression given is that Lloyd's is ashamed of its past and will embrace anything that new capital suggests," it says.
CBSL suggest it is sensible to allow the current set-up of both Names and corporate capital first introduced in 1994, to be assimilated and tested before doing away with the annual venture.
"A period of reflection now might, in retrospect, be seen as a sensible precaution," it concludes.
